intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GAD1 gene (605363) on chromosome 2q31.

checks.explanation: Paper reports homozygous and compound heterozygous GAD1 variants causing developmental and epileptic encephalopathy; DEE89 is the OMIM label.

paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder. Seizures begin in the first months of life, mainly as epileptic spasms, myoclonic seizures, or focal motor seizures, and the EEG often shows a suppression-burst pattern or hypsarrhythmia. Patients have severe developmental delay and intellectual disability with abnormal muscle tone. Some patients also have features outside the central nervous system, including cleft palate, omphalocele, talipes equinovarus, joint contractures, and dysmorphic facial features (Chatron et al., 2020; Neuray et al., 2020).

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients from 6 consanguineous families with a syndromic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy that began in the neonatal period. In all 11 patients, seizures began in the first 2 months of life, mainly as epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures. Seven of 8 patients who had neonatal EEGs showed a suppression-burst or burst-attenuation pattern, and the 2 patients first recorded later showed hypsarrhythmia. The authors described increased muscle tone as a core feature, often together with axial hypotonia.

paragraphs.text: In Family A of Chatron et al. (2020), the parents were healthy first cousins of Algerian origin. Their first child, a boy (case 1), had a cleft soft palate. He was first referred at 5 months of age with developmental regression, loss of visual contact, opisthotonus, and axial hypotonia. He had epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia. At 6 years of age he could not sit unassisted, had spastic tetraparesis with limited extension of the knees and elbows, and did not communicate verbally. He also had scoliosis and profound intellectual disability, and his brain MRI was normal. His sister (case 2) also had a cleft soft palate. At 2 days of age she was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit with episodes of eye revulsion, cyanosis, and spasm-like movements, and her EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern. At 26 months of age she had severe developmental delay, axial hypotonia, no head control, segmental hypertonia with limited extension of the knees, no visual contact, abnormal eye movements, and no verbal communication.

paragraphs.text: Family B of Chatron et al. (2020) was a consanguineous Egyptian family. In case 3, a girl, a detailed prenatal scan showed an omphalocele containing liver, intestinal atresia, and right talipes equinovarus, and polyhydramnios was also present. She was born at term by cesarean section with a birth weight of 2.900 kg and had an omphalocele and a cleft soft palate. From 2 weeks of age she had seizures in the form of eye twitches and epileptic spasms. Her EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern that evolved to hypsarrhythmia. Her developmental delay was severe. Brain imaging showed a hypoplastic corpus callosum, cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, and enlarged lateral ventricles. Her dysmorphic features were hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, microretrognathia, low-set, abnormally shaped ears, and neck webbing. She also had multiple skin hemangiomas, limited range of movement in all joints, camptodactyly, rocker-bottom feet, scoliosis, a large clitoris with hypoplastic labia, and spasticity. She died at 2 years of age from failure to thrive and respiratory infection. Her similarly affected brother (case 4) had an omphalocele and bilateral talipes equinovarus at birth. He had seizures from 2 weeks of age (eye twitches and epileptic spasms), arthrogryposis, failure to thrive, global developmental delay, and dysmorphic features similar to his sister's, but no cleft palate. He died at 4 years of age from pulmonary infection and severe growth retardation.

paragraphs.text: In Family C of Chatron et al. (2020), the parents were apparently healthy Turkish first cousins. Their first child, a girl (case 5), developed eyelid myoclonia at 2 weeks of age and, 1 week later, myoclonic seizures of the upper limbs. She later had generalized tonic-clonic seizures and refractory epilepsy. Her EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern and photosensitivity. At 12 years of age she had profound intellectual disability and no speech. She had been generally hypotonic in infancy and later had tetraparesis with increased muscle tone. She also had a cleft palate, left-sided talipes, conductive hearing loss, and recurrent fever episodes without signs of infection, and her brain MRI was normal. Her brother (case 6) had a similar phenotype, with refractory myoclonic, tonic, and tonic-clonic seizures from the first day of life, a cleft palate, a suppression-burst EEG, and a normal brain MRI. His seizures worsened on a ketogenic diet. He died from refractory seizures at 2 years of age, when he had profound intellectual disability and tetraparesis with increased muscle tone.

paragraphs.text: In Family D of Chatron et al. (2020), the parents were healthy Iranian second cousins, and there was a family history of epilepsy and developmental delay. Case 7, a boy and the second child of these parents, had myoclonic seizures within 1 day of birth and an EEG showing dysrhythmia. His seizures evolved into epileptic spasms. He had profound developmental delay and could not walk, and imaging showed prominent inner liquor spaces. His muscle tone was initially reduced, and he later developed spasticity, dystonia, and scoliosis. His dysmorphic features included low-set ears, a broad nasal bridge, mild hypertelorism, and a thin upper lip. Case 8, a girl from the same family, had epileptic spasms and myoclonic seizures at 7 days of age. Her EEG showed burst attenuation at first and scattered sharp waves later. At 15 months of age she could roll onto her sides but could not sit unsupported, and her head circumference was 44 cm (1.2 cm below the 3rd centile). She had axial hypotonia and mild dystonia. A cervical notch seen on brain MRI was considered likely unrelated to the GAD1 variant.

paragraphs.text: Family E of Chatron et al. (2020) was a consanguineous Turkish family. Case 9, a boy, was referred at 2 months of age for facial dysmorphism, developmental delay, cleft palate, Hirschsprung disease, and pes equinovarus. Epileptic spasms were seen on examination. In retrospect they had been present from 1 month of age, and his EEG showed hypsarrhythmia. Other findings were flexion contractures of the elbows and knees, upslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, microretrognathia, low-set ears, cervical and axillary webbing, umbilical hernia, hepatomegaly, intrauterine hydrocephalus, an atlantoaxial anomaly, nystagmus, alternating esotropia, bilateral pale optic discs, recurrent aspiration pneumonia, atrial septal defect, nephrocalcinosis, and sparse hair and eyebrows. His audiogram was normal at birth, but he failed a hearing test at 1 year of age. At 15 months of age he had no head control or eye contact, axial hypotonia, and limb spasticity. His older brother (case 10) was born at 29 weeks' gestation with cleft palate, short neck, narrow thorax, and pes equinovarus. He had myoclonic seizures and congenital heart disease (a large patent ductus arteriosus, a small atrial septal defect, and moderate pulmonary hypertension), as well as abdominal distension. He died on postnatal day 9 from sepsis.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) also tested some of the variants functionally or by modeling. In Family A, cDNA analysis showed that the c.1414-1G-C variant abolished normal splicing: there was no normal mRNA product, and 3 aberrant isoforms were present (skipping of exon 15, retention of 76 bases of intron 14, or deletion of the first 7 bases of exon 15). In a cell-free expression system, the lys232del GAD67 variant from Family B was expressed at a level comparable to wildtype. The authors noted that this result did not exclude a splicing effect predicted in silico. They considered the variant pathogenic because the family reproduced the cleft palate and omphalocele of the knockout mouse, although loss of function was not formally demonstrated. Structural modeling predicted that the E509K variant, which affects a highly conserved residue in the pyridoxal-dependent decarboxylase domain, would disrupt salt bridges with arg316, lys318, and lys389 and would no longer fit into the domain core.
